issues.legal_issue: Judicial review of a search authorization is limited to examining whether the recorded belief was bona fide and relevant, and does not permit the court to reassess the sufficiency of the reasons.
material_facts: The authorization for search and seizure was challenged in a writ petition, and the recorded reasons were placed before the courts.
The High Court examined the material and concluded that the statutory conditions for the search were not met.

The Supreme Court found that the Revenue had recorded reasons based on information concerning the transactions and the investigation, and held that the High Court had impermissibly interfered with the authorization.
issues.conclusion: A reviewing court may examine whether information existed, whether the recorded reasons had a rational connection to the belief, and whether the belief was bona fide rather than a pretence; it cannot reassess the sufficiency or adequacy of those reasons as if hearing an appeal on the merits.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 132(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, the authority must possess information supporting a bona fide belief connected to the statutory grounds for search. The belief is administrative, not judicial or quasi-judicial. Applying the principles in S. Narayanappa v. CIT, ITO v. Lakhmani Mewal Das, ITO v. Seth Brothers, Partap Singh v. Director of Enforcement, Union of India v. Agarwal Iron Industries, and Spacewood Furnishers (P) Ltd., the court may examine the existence, good faith, and relevance of the reasons, but not their sufficiency. Tata Cellular v. Union of India supports judicial restraint in reviewing administrative decisions.

predicates.search_authorization_challenged_in_writ: A person challenged an administrative authorization to conduct a search and seizure in a writ proceeding.
predicates.authority_recorded_reasons: The authorizing official recorded reasons for forming the belief that a search was warranted.
predicates.reasons_based_on_information_in_authorit: The official formed the belief using information that was in the official’s possession.

issues.definition: When a recorded search authorization is challenged in a writ proceeding and the official relied on information in the official’s possession, review tests good faith and relevance rather than the sufficiency of the reasons.

issues.legal_issue: A search authorization may be supported by a bona fide belief that a person will not produce relevant records and that funds in the person’s possession may represent undisclosed income, even where the underlying transaction was repaid and its interest was reported.
material_facts: The assessee advanced a substantial loan to a company soon after becoming its director and ceased to be a director shortly afterward.
The company had no established business when it raised substantial loans, and it was associated with significant suspicious cash deposits and transactions involving other persons and companies.
The loan was repaid in instalments, the mortgage securing it was released, and the assessee reported the interest income, which was taxed.
The Revenue suspected that the loan was an accommodation entry and sought to trace the source and movement of the funds.
The Revenue had a basis to believe that issuing a summons could alert the assessee to the investigation and that relevant records might not be produced.
issues.conclusion: The recorded reasons supported the statutory grounds for search, and the authorization was valid; the High Court was not justified in setting it aside.
issues.legal_principle: Section 132(1)(b) permits authorization where information supports a reasonable belief that a person will not produce records useful or relevant to proceedings, even if summoned. Section 132(1)(c) permits authorization where information supports a reasonable belief that a person possesses money representing wholly or partly undisclosed income or property. The belief need not be a final conclusion about undisclosed income, and a search need not ultimately yield incriminating material. Under S. Narayanappa, ITO v. Lakhmani Mewal Das, Partap Singh, and Seth Brothers, the belief must be bona fide and rationally connected to the material; its sufficiency is not for the court to reassess.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_search_authorization and short_term_loan_to_unconnected_borrower and borrower_lacked_established_business and borrower_linked_to_suspicious_financial_activity and fund_source_under_investigation and authority_reasonably_anticipated_nonproduction

predicates.appeal_challenges_search_authorization: An appeal challenges a lower court’s decision setting aside an authorization to conduct a search.
predicates.short_term_loan_to_unconnected_borrower: A person advanced funds for a limited period to a borrower with whom the person had no established financial dealings.
predicates.borrower_lacked_established_business: The borrower had no established business or market goodwill when it received the funds.
predicates.borrower_linked_to_suspicious_financial_: The borrower was linked to suspicious cash deposits or a wider pattern of financial transactions under investigation.
predicates.fund_source_under_investigation: The investigating authority was seeking to trace the source or movement of the funds advanced by the person.
predicates.authority_reasonably_anticipated_nonprod: The authority had a bona fide basis to believe that the person would not produce relevant records if given notice.

issues.definition: If an appeal concerns a search authorization and the authority had the stated transaction-related information and a reasonable basis to anticipate nonproduction, the authorization is valid.

issues.legal_issue: Reasons recorded to support a search authorization need not be disclosed to the person searched at the authorization stage.
material_facts: The satisfaction note recording the reasons for the search was not supplied to the assessee.
The recorded reasons were produced before the High Court and the Supreme Court.
The governing explanation applied retrospectively and stated that recorded reasons to believe were not to be disclosed to any person or authority or the Appellate Tribunal.
issues.conclusion: The recorded reasons did not have to be disclosed to the assessee when the search authorization was issued.
issues.legal_principle: The Explanation to Section 132(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961, inserted by the Finance Act, 2017 with retrospective effect, provides that recorded reasons to believe are not to be disclosed to any person, authority, or the Appellate Tribunal. Spacewood Furnishers (P) Ltd. also recognizes that an assessee has no right to inspection or communication of the reasons at the authorization stage.

predicates.search_authorization_stage: The search authorization has been issued and the search is at its authorization stage.
predicates.reasons_recorded_in_satisfaction_note: The authorizing officials recorded their reasons for the belief supporting the search in a satisfaction note.

issues.definition: At the authorization stage, when reasons supporting a search have been recorded in a satisfaction note, those reasons need not be disclosed to the searched person.
